subject: ela
intro: Each item below gives you a written passage and then describes an audio, video, or live version of that same text in words. Read both carefully. Then compare the two experiences, judge which medium serves a moment better, or explain how the version's choices shift the meaning or feeling. Support every answer with specific details from both the text and the described version.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs for the last time. Forty years he had kept the lamp burning, and tomorrow a machine would take his place. At the top he wiped the great lens with his sleeve, the way he always had. He did not cry. He only stood and watched the dark water, listening to the waves he had listened to all his life. Then he turned off the lamp himself, so that no machine could.' In a film version, the camera holds on the keeper's face in total silence as he reaches the top, then the only sound is the slow drip of water and a single deep note of music as the lamp goes dark. The film cuts the line 'He did not cry.' Compare the two experiences of this moment, and explain how the film's choices change what the audience understands compared with the text.
items.answer: The text and film both deliver the keeper's quiet, dignified goodbye and his choice to shut off the lamp himself, but they reveal his feelings differently. The text states plainly 'He did not cry,' directly telling the reader he holds his emotion in, and it gives his exact inner history through the narrator. The film cuts that line and instead holds silently on his face with only a water drip and a single deep music note, so the audience must read his held-back grief from his expression and the heavy quiet rather than being told it. The film adds sound and a visible face the print cannot show, while the text keeps the keeper's restraint as a stated fact that the film turns into something the viewer has to feel and interpret.

steps: Find the shared core: both versions show the keeper saying goodbye after forty years and turning off the lamp himself.
Name what the text does best: the line 'He did not cry' is direct narration that states his restraint, and the narrator supplies his forty-year history in words.
Name what the film adds and changes: it cuts 'He did not cry,' and uses a silent held shot of his face, a water drip, and one deep music note, tools of sound and image that print cannot provide.

Connect choice to effect: by removing the stated line and lingering on his face in silence, the film makes the audience infer his held-in grief from his expression and the heavy quiet instead of being told it.
State the comparison: the text tells the feeling directly while the film shows it and asks the viewer to feel and interpret it.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'Nadia opened the envelope with shaking hands. The letter said she had won the scholarship. She read it three times to be sure. Inside, she felt her whole future swing open like a door. But when her brother walked in, she folded the letter fast and said it was nothing, just a flyer. She was not ready to share it, not yet. She wanted to hold the good news alone a little longer.' A live stage version performs this scene with the actor playing Nadia clutching the letter to her chest and beaming when she is alone, then snapping into a blank, careless face the instant her brother enters, dropping her voice flat as she says 'it was nothing.' For showing why Nadia hides the letter from her brother, judge which version is more effective, and justify your answer with details from both.
items.answer: The written text is more effective for showing why Nadia hides the letter. The text states her exact reason in words: 'She was not ready to share it, not yet. She wanted to hold the good news alone a little longer.' That inner thought is something only print can deliver directly. The live version shows her hiding it well, the beaming face when alone snapping to a blank, careless look and a flat voice when her brother enters, so the audience clearly sees that she is hiding something and acting. But the stage cannot reveal the unspoken reason inside her, that she wants to keep the joy to herself a while longer, which the text gives outright. So the performance powerfully shows the behavior, while the text better explains the motive behind it.

steps: Identify the question's focus: why Nadia hides the letter, which is a matter of inner motive.
Find the text's tool: the narration states her reason directly, that she is not ready to share and wants to hold the news alone a little longer.
Find the stage version's tools: the beaming-to-blank face switch and flat voice that show she is acting and concealing, visible behavior print cannot show.
Weigh them against the purpose: the motive is an unspoken thought, which the live performance can suggest but cannot state, while print delivers it exactly.
Justify the judgment: the text wins for revealing the why, citing the stated inner reason, even though the stage better shows the act of hiding.

items.prompt: Read this complete short poem: 'The Last Bell' — 'The schoolyard empties, slow, then fast, / a tide of feet that will not last. / One swing still moves where no one swings, / one cold chain creaks, one sparrow sings. / Summer waits beyond the gate, / and yet I find I want to wait. / The bell that freed us rang too soon; / I miss it now this afternoon.' An audio version reads the poem in a young, wistful voice, slowing down on the last two lines, while faint sounds play behind the words: distant shouting children that fade to silence, a single creaking chain, and one bird call. Compare reading this poem silently with hearing the audio version, naming one important similarity and one important difference, and explain how the audio's choices affect the listener.
items.answer: Both the silent reading and the audio version deliver the same bittersweet idea: the speaker is surprisingly sad that the school year is over and misses the bell that set everyone free. That is the shared meaning. The key difference is that reading silently, the listener notices the rhyme and the repeated images of the swing, chain, and sparrow and pictures the empty schoolyard alone, while the audio adds real sounds, fading children's shouts, a creaking chain, and a bird call, plus a wistful voice that slows on the last two lines. Those choices affect the listener by making the emptiness audible: the shouts fading to silence and the lone creak let the listener hear the yard grow quiet, and the slowing voice stretches the regret in 'I miss it now this afternoon,' making the wistful feeling stronger than the words alone.

steps: State the shared meaning: in both, the speaker feels unexpected sadness at the year ending and misses the bell.
Name a similarity grounded in both: the bittersweet idea and the images of swing, chain, and sparrow are present either way.
Name a difference: print gives rhyme and reader-imagined images, while audio supplies actual fading shouts, a creaking chain, a bird call, and a wistful slowing voice.
Connect the audio choices to effect: the fading sounds make the yard's emptiness audible and the slowed last lines stretch the regret.
Conclude the comparison: the audio intensifies the wistful feeling that the silent reader only pictures.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'Coach Diaz gathered the team after the loss. "You played hard," he said. "I am proud of every one of you." His words were kind. But inside, the players could feel something else under the kindness, a disappointment he was too good a coach to say aloud. They had thrown the game away in the final minute, and they knew it, and they knew he knew it too.' In a film version, the actor playing Coach Diaz says the kind words while looking down at the floor, his jaw tight, and pauses a long beat before 'I am proud,' as if forcing it out. A low, sad string note plays under his voice. The film keeps every spoken word but cuts the narration about the disappointment under the kindness. Analyze how the film conveys the same hidden disappointment the text describes, and explain what each medium does that the other cannot.
items.answer: The text and film both get across that Coach Diaz is kind on the surface but quietly disappointed underneath. The text does it by directly naming the inner truth: the players feel 'a disappointment he was too good a coach to say aloud,' and the narrator tells us they all silently know it. The film cannot speak that hidden thought, so it shows it through performance and sound instead: the actor looks down with a tight jaw, pauses a long beat before 'I am proud' as if forcing it, and a low sad string note plays under the kind words. What the text does that the film cannot is state the unspoken feeling outright through narration. What the film does that the text cannot is let the audience hear the strained voice and music and see the body language, so they sense the disappointment directly instead of being told about it.

steps: Identify the shared idea: kind words on the surface, hidden disappointment underneath.
Find the text's method: narration directly states the disappointment 'he was too good a coach to say aloud' and that the players silently know.
Find the film's methods: downcast look, tight jaw, a forced pause before 'I am proud,' and a low sad string note, which replace the cut narration.
Name what only the text can do: state the unspoken inner feeling in words.
Name what only the film can do: deliver tone of voice, music, and body language so the viewer senses the feeling directly rather than being told.

items.prompt: Read this drama excerpt: 'JONAH: I'm leaving on the morning train. / MOTHER: You'll write? / JONAH: Every week. / MOTHER: You always say that. / (JONAH does not answer.)' In a live performance, the actor playing Jonah lets the silence after 'You always say that' stretch for several seconds while he looks away, and then quietly picks up his mother's hand and holds it instead of speaking. The stage lights dim slowly during this silence. The script's only direction is '(JONAH does not answer.)' Explain how the live version interprets the silence in the script, and judge whether its added choices strengthen or weaken the moment, with reasons from both.
items.answer: The script gives almost nothing for the silence, only the bare stage direction '(JONAH does not answer.)', leaving the reader to decide what his silence means. The live version interprets that silence as tender and sorrowful: the actor lets it stretch, looks away, and then holds his mother's hand instead of speaking while the lights dim slowly. These added choices strengthen the moment. The held hand and the dimming lights turn an empty pause on the page into a clear, wordless answer: Jonah cannot promise he will keep writing, and he loves her anyway. The text leaves his feeling open, which a reader might miss, but the staging makes his regret and affection visible without changing his words. The added gesture and light fill the silence with meaning the script only hints at, so the performance deepens rather than weakens the scene.

steps: Find what the script supplies: only the direction '(JONAH does not answer.)', an open, undefined silence.
Identify the live version's interpretation: a stretched silence, looking away, holding the mother's hand, and slowly dimming lights.
Judge the effect: these choices read the silence as tender regret and a wordless admission that he may not keep his promise.
Give reasons from both: the script leaves the meaning open and easy to miss, while the staging makes the feeling visible without altering the spoken words.
Conclude: the added gesture and lighting strengthen the moment by filling the silence the text only hints at.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The storm came in three parts. First the wind, bending the young trees flat. Then the rain, so hard the street turned into a river. Last the thunder, close and enormous, rattling every window in the house. Mara counted the seconds between the lightning and the boom, the way her father had taught her, and felt safer for the counting.' An audio version of this passage reorders the events for drama: it plays a sudden enormous thunderclap first, before any narration, then has the narrator read the passage from the beginning. Wind and rain sounds build under the words. Explain what the audio version changes by reordering the storm, and analyze how that change affects the listener compared with reading the passage in order.
items.answer: The text presents the storm in a careful order, wind first, then rain, then thunder last, and ends on Mara calming herself by counting, so the reader moves from chaos toward safety. The audio version reorders this by playing a huge thunderclap before any words, then reading the passage from the start. This change, which the print does not have, hits the listener with the storm's most frightening sound first, so the listener feels startled and on edge before learning anything about Mara. Reading in order, the reader builds up to the thunder and then settles into Mara's calm counting, ending reassured. The reordered audio puts the scare up front, so even as the narrator later describes Mara feeling safer, the listener still carries the shock of that opening boom. The reorder trades the text's steady build and calming close for an immediate jolt of fear.

steps: Note the text's order and arc: wind, rain, thunder, then Mara counting and feeling safer, moving from chaos to calm.
Identify the audio's change: it plays the loud thunderclap first, before the narration, reordering the events.
Name the added tools: the real thunderclap and building wind and rain sounds, which print cannot provide.
Analyze the effect: starting with the scariest sound startles the listener up front, unlike the text's gradual build.
Compare the endings: the text closes on reassurance, but the reordered audio leaves the opening shock lingering even through Mara's calm.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'Everyone said the new girl, Priya, was stuck-up. She never spoke in class and ate lunch alone, staring at her book. But the truth was that Priya had moved three times that year, and she had stopped trying to make friends only because it hurt too much to lose them again. She wanted to belong more than anyone. She just no longer believed she would.' A film version shows Priya silent and alone, reading at a corner table while other students laugh together across the room. The camera lingers on her blank face. There is no narration; viewers see only what she does, not what she thinks. Judge which version more fairly shows who Priya really is, and justify your answer with details from both.
items.answer: The written text far more fairly shows who Priya really is. The text reveals her hidden truth in words: she has moved three times, she stopped making friends only because losing them hurt too much, and she 'wanted to belong more than anyone' but no longer believes she will. The film shows only her outward behavior, sitting silent and alone with a blank face while others laugh, which is exactly the surface that makes everyone wrongly call her stuck-up. With no narration, a viewer sees what she does but not what she thinks, so the film risks repeating the same unfair judgment the text corrects. Print is more effective here because it can directly reveal her inner thoughts and history, while the camera can only show her actions and leaves her real reasons hidden.

steps: Identify the focus: showing who Priya really is, which depends on her hidden inner truth.
Find the text's tool: narration states her history of moving and her real reason for withdrawing, plus her wish to belong.
Find the film's limits: it shows only silent, blank behavior and others laughing, with no narration of her thoughts.
Connect to the misjudgment: the film's surface matches the very 'stuck-up' impression the text exists to correct.
Justify the judgment: the text wins because only print directly reveals her inner reasons, while the camera shows actions alone.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'Grandpa told the story of the great flood every winter, and every winter it grew. One year the water was knee-deep; the next it reached the rooftops. The boat he rowed got bigger; the fish he caught got stranger. We all knew the story changed. We did not mind. We loved watching him remember, even the parts he was inventing on the spot.' An audio version performs Grandpa with a warm, playful voice that grows more excited and exaggerated as the story gets wilder, with gentle laughter from listeners mixed in at the most unlikely details. Analyze how the audio version uses voice and added sound to convey the family's attitude toward Grandpa's story, and compare that with how the text conveys it.
items.answer: Both versions convey that the family knows Grandpa exaggerates and loves him for it, but they do it with different tools. The text states the attitude directly: 'We all knew the story changed. We did not mind,' and 'We loved watching him remember, even the parts he was inventing on the spot.' The audio cannot narrate that thought, so it conveys the same warmth through voice and sound: Grandpa's warm, playful tone grows more excited and exaggerated as the tale gets wilder, and gentle listener laughter is mixed in at the most unlikely details. That laughter, a sound print cannot supply, lets the audience hear the family's fond amusement rather than be told about it, and the swelling voice makes Grandpa's joy in storytelling audible. So the text names the loving attitude in words, while the audio lets the listener hear it in the playful voice and the affectionate laughter.

steps: Identify the shared idea: the family knows the story grows and loves Grandpa for telling it anyway.
Find the text's method: direct statements 'We did not mind' and 'We loved watching him remember.'
Find the audio's tools: a warm playful voice that grows excited and exaggerated, plus mixed-in gentle listener laughter.
Analyze the effect: the laughter and swelling voice let the audience hear the family's fond amusement instead of being told it.
Compare: print states the attitude, audio makes it audible through performance and sound.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The magician pulled back the curtain, and the whole crowd gasped. Whatever they saw, it was wonderful. Children pointed. A woman near the front pressed her hand to her mouth. Even the bored ticket-taker leaned in. The narrator never tells us what was behind the curtain. We are left to imagine the most amazing thing we can.' A film version of this scene reveals exactly what is behind the curtain: a white horse with a glittering silver mane, standing under a spotlight. The crowd in the film gasps just as in the text. Compare what the text and the film each leave to the imagination, and judge which choice is better for this particular moment, with reasons from both.
items.answer: The text deliberately hides what is behind the curtain. It describes only the crowd's gasps and reactions and then says outright, 'The narrator never tells us what was behind the curtain. We are left to imagine the most amazing thing we can.' That blank space invites every reader to picture their own most wonderful sight. The film cannot leave that gap; it fixes one image for everyone, a white horse with a glittering silver mane under a spotlight. For this particular moment, the text's choice is better. The whole point of the scene is the limitless wonder each person imagines, and a film image, however pretty, replaces that boundless possibility with one fixed picture that might disappoint a viewer who imagined something grander. The film gives a clear, shared image, but the text's refusal to show gives each reader the most amazing thing they can dream, which fits this moment's purpose far better.

steps: Identify the text's key choice: it withholds the reveal and explicitly invites readers to imagine the most amazing thing.
Identify the film's choice: it shows one fixed image, a white horse with a silver mane under a spotlight.
Frame the moment's purpose: the scene is about boundless, personal wonder.
Weigh the choices: a single fixed image cannot match every viewer's imagined ideal and may disappoint.
Justify the judgment: the text serves this moment better because leaving it blank preserves limitless wonder, while the film locks in one picture.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'When the verdict was read, the courtroom held its breath. Tomas had waited two years for this. "Not guilty," the judge said. For a moment Tomas felt nothing at all, as if the words had not reached him yet. Then, all at once, his knees went weak and his eyes burned, and he understood that it was finally over. He had imagined this moment a thousand times. He had never once imagined the silence inside himself before the relief arrived.' A live stage version performs this with the actor playing Tomas standing perfectly still and expressionless for a long, uncomfortable beat after 'Not guilty,' then suddenly gripping the table and lowering his head as the lights brighten. No words describe his feelings; the audience watches his body. Analyze how the staging captures the two-stage reaction in the text, and explain what the text reveals that the staging cannot.
items.answer: The text describes a two-stage reaction: first Tomas feels 'nothing at all, as if the words had not reached him yet,' and only then, 'all at once,' his knees weaken and his eyes burn with relief. The staging captures this same two-stage shape through the body: the actor stands perfectly still and expressionless for a long, uncomfortable beat, matching the numb first stage, then suddenly grips the table and lowers his head as the lights brighten, matching the rush of relief. The brightening lights mark the shift the way the word 'Then' does in the text. What the text reveals that the staging cannot is Tomas's exact inner thought: that he had imagined this moment a thousand times but 'never once imagined the silence inside himself before the relief arrived.' The stage can show the still beat, but only the narration can tell us that the numbness itself surprised him.

steps: Identify the text's two stages: an initial numbness where he feels nothing, then a sudden flood of relief.
Match the staging to each stage: the still, expressionless beat for the numbness, then the grip and lowered head with brightening lights for the relief.
Note how the version marks the shift: the lights brighten where the text uses 'Then, all at once.'
Name what only the text reveals: his reflection that he never imagined the inner silence that came before the relief.
Conclude: the staging shows the outward two-stage reaction, but only narration delivers the surprising inner thought.

items.prompt: Read this complete short poem: 'Crossing' — 'The river is not deep, they say, / just step from grey stone to grey stone. / But water moving has a way / of making solid ground unknown. / I set one foot. The cold bites through. / Behind me, easy. Far ahead, / the other bank, the thing to do. / I stand here in the middle, / dread / and daring tangled in my chest, / and choose, at last, the forward stone.' An audio version reads this in a tense, careful voice, pausing a long time at the single word 'dread' set alone on its line, while the steady rush of moving water plays under the whole poem and goes suddenly quiet at the final line. Compare reading this poem on the page with hearing the audio version, and analyze how the audio's pause and the sudden quiet shape the listener's understanding of the speaker's choice.
items.answer: On the page, the reader sees the poem's shape, including the word 'dread' set alone on its own line, and notices the speaker's fear and courage 'tangled' as they pause in the middle of the river before choosing the forward stone. The audio adds tools print lacks: a tense, careful voice, a long pause on the isolated word 'dread,' and the steady rush of water under the whole poem that goes suddenly quiet at the last line. These choices shape the listener's understanding of the choice. The long pause on 'dread' makes the listener feel the speaker's fear hang in the air, matching the lonely placement of the word on the page but stretching it in time. The sudden quiet of the water at the final line marks the moment of decision, as if the world stills the instant the speaker commits to the forward stone. So the audio turns the visual gap and the rushing river into heard hesitation and a heard moment of resolve.

steps: Note the page experience: the reader sees 'dread' isolated on its line and reads the tangle of fear and courage before the choice.
Identify the audio's tools: a tense voice, a long pause on 'dread,' rushing water throughout, and sudden quiet at the last line.
Analyze the pause: holding on 'dread' stretches the speaker's fear in time, going beyond the visual isolation of the word.
Analyze the sudden quiet: the water stopping at the final line marks the instant of decision, as if the world stills.
Compare: the audio converts the poem's visual gap and rushing river into heard hesitation and a heard moment of resolve.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The twins were nothing alike. Sam was loud, always first to speak, always sure. Lena was quiet and watched everything. When their dog ran into the road, it was loud Sam who froze and quiet Lena who darted out and pulled the dog back by its collar, both of them tumbling safe onto the grass. That was the day everyone learned that being quiet is not the same as being afraid.' A film version shows the scene of the dog in the road without any narration. Viewers see Sam freeze, Lena dash out and grab the dog, and the two roll safely onto the grass. The film keeps the action but includes no version of the final sentence about quiet not being the same as fear. Judge whether the film fully delivers the passage's meaning, and justify your answer using details from both.
items.answer: The film delivers the events of the passage but not its full meaning. It accurately shows the action the text describes: Sam freezing, Lena dashing out to grab the dog, and the two rolling safely onto the grass, so the audience can see that the quiet twin acted while the loud one did not. What the film leaves out is the text's stated lesson, the final sentence 'being quiet is not the same as being afraid.' Without narration, a viewer can infer that idea from watching Lena act, but the film never states it, so the point is suggested rather than made plain. The text both shows the rescue and names its meaning directly, while the film shows the rescue and trusts the viewer to draw the conclusion. The film delivers the story's surface but relies on inference for the theme the text spells out.

steps: Separate events from meaning: the passage shows a rescue and then states a lesson about quietness and fear.
Confirm the film shows the events: Sam freezes, Lena grabs the dog, both tumble safely onto the grass.
Identify what the film omits: the final stated lesson that being quiet is not the same as being afraid.
Analyze the gap: without narration the theme must be inferred from the action rather than stated.
Justify the judgment: the film delivers the surface story but not the explicit meaning, which only the text states outright.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The marketplace was the loudest place Ravi knew. Sellers shouted prices over one another. A man banged a drum to draw a crowd. Bells on the goats jingled, a baby wailed, and somewhere a flute played a thin, hopeful tune that no one but Ravi seemed to hear. Ravi closed his eyes and picked out each sound, one by one, like threads in a rope. To everyone else it was noise. To him it was a kind of music.' An audio version layers all these sounds at once at full volume, shouting, a drum, jingling bells, a crying baby, and faintly under it all, a thin flute, exactly as described. Then it lowers every sound except the flute, which rises clear for a moment. Compare how the text and the audio each help you understand Ravi's special way of hearing the marketplace, and analyze the effect of the audio lowering the other sounds to lift the flute.
items.answer: Both versions help us understand that Ravi hears music where others hear only noise, but through different means. The text tells us his experience in words: he closes his eyes and picks out each sound 'one by one, like threads in a rope,' and notices the thin flute 'that no one but Ravi seemed to hear.' The audio gives the listener the actual chaos, layering shouting, a drum, bells, and a crying baby at full volume so we feel the overwhelming noise, sounds print can only describe. Then it lowers every sound except the flute, which rises clear. That choice lets the listener share Ravi's special hearing directly: just as he singles out the flute thread, the audio singles it out for us, so we briefly hear the marketplace the way he does. The text explains his way of listening, while the audio makes us experience it by pulling the flute out of the noise.

steps: Identify the shared idea: Ravi hears music in the marketplace where others hear only noise.
Find the text's method: it states that he picks sounds out 'one by one, like threads in a rope' and hears a flute no one else notices.
Find the audio's tools: it layers all the real sounds at full volume, then lowers everything except the rising flute.
Analyze the lowering effect: pulling the flute out of the noise lets the listener single it out just as Ravi does.
Compare: the text explains his way of hearing, while the audio makes the listener experience it directly.

items.prompt: Read this drama excerpt: 'CAPTAIN: We turn back at dawn. / SAILOR: The men won't like it. / CAPTAIN: The men will be alive. That is the like I care about. / SAILOR: And you? Will you forgive yourself for turning back so close? / CAPTAIN: (long pause) Ask me in twenty years.' A live performance stages the captain's final line with the actor turning slowly toward the dark sea, gripping the rail, and speaking 'Ask me in twenty years' in a low, rough voice while a cold wind sound rises and the stage lights narrow to a single spotlight on him. The script gives only '(long pause)' before the line. Analyze how the staging interprets the captain's line, and judge whether the added sound and lighting deepen or distract from the moment, with reasons from both.
items.answer: The script offers only the bare direction '(long pause)' before 'Ask me in twenty years,' leaving the captain's feeling open on the page. The live performance interprets that line as full of private regret and lonely burden: the actor turns toward the dark sea, grips the rail, and speaks low and rough while a cold wind rises and the lights narrow to a single spotlight on him. These added choices deepen the moment rather than distract. The spotlight isolating the captain matches the loneliness of a leader who must carry a hard choice alone, and the cold wind and rough voice make the sea's danger and his weariness felt, so the audience understands that turning back will haunt him even though it saves the men. The text states only the pause and the words, but the staging gives that silence a clear weight of regret. The sound and lighting fit the line's meaning, so they strengthen the scene instead of pulling attention from it.

steps: Find what the script supplies: only '(long pause)' and the spoken line, leaving the feeling undefined.
Identify the staging's interpretation: turning to the dark sea, gripping the rail, a low rough voice, rising cold wind, and a narrowing spotlight.
Analyze how each choice reads the line: the spotlight signals lonely burden, the wind and rough voice signal danger and weariness and lingering regret.
Judge deepen vs. distract: the choices all point to the captain's private regret and isolation, matching the line's meaning.
Justify with both: the script leaves the pause empty, while the staging fills it with fitting weight, so the additions strengthen rather than distract.

items.prompt: Read this passage: 'The letter from her old friend sat unopened on the table for a week. Every time Dana passed it, she thought about the fight that had ended things, the words she wished she could take back. She wanted to open it. She was afraid of what it might say. On the eighth day she finally tore it open, and inside, in her friend's familiar handwriting, were just three words: "I miss you." Dana sat down slowly and let herself cry, half from sorrow and half from relief.' Two versions exist. A film shows the unopened letter, Dana passing it again and again, and finally opening it; the camera shows the three words and Dana crying, but no narration tells her thoughts. An audio version reads every word of the passage in a gentle voice but has no images. Compare what each version captures and misses, and judge which is better suited to this particular story, with reasons from both.
items.answer: The two versions capture different parts of this story. The film captures the outward situation vividly: it shows the letter sitting unopened, Dana passing it again and again, the three words 'I miss you' in the friend's handwriting, and Dana crying, all images print can only describe. But with no narration it misses her inner experience, that she fears what the letter says, that she wishes she could take back the words from the fight, and that her tears are 'half from sorrow and half from relief.' The audio keeps every word, including those inner thoughts, so it captures her hidden feelings and her mixed tears, but it has no images, so the listener must picture the unopened letter and the handwriting. For this particular story, the audio is better suited, because the heart of the passage is Dana's inner conflict, her fear, her regret, and the mix of sorrow and relief, which only the narrated words deliver. The film shows the moment, but the audio carries the feelings that give the moment meaning.

steps: List what the film captures: the unopened letter, Dana passing it, the three words in familiar handwriting, and her crying, all images.
List what the film misses: her fear, her regret over the fight, and that her tears are half sorrow and half relief, since it has no narration.
List what the audio captures and misses: it keeps every word including the inner thoughts but provides no images.
Identify the story's heart: Dana's inner conflict and her mixed feelings of sorrow and relief.
Justify the judgment: the audio is better suited because only the narrated words deliver the inner feelings that give the moment its meaning, while the film shows the scene but not the thoughts.
